articles.title: ‘Try to eat really well, 80% of the time’: nutrition expert says healthy eating is easier than you think
articles.summary: Christopher Gardner, the author of Food Sense and director of nutrition studies at Stanford, says we have overcomplicated the question of what to eat. Finally, some good news: eating well is more straightforward than you think.
body: In the age of social media and wellness grift, we’ve overcomplicated the question of what to eat, he says.

In 2023, Gardner was invited to serve on the US government’s dietary guidelines advisory committee, reviewing the official guidelines for healthy eating and recommending updates. “It was quite an honour to be asked,” remembers Gardner. It was also “a tonne of work”.

Gardner was more than up for the task. He has researched nutrition for more than 30 years, regularly advising official bodies on the latest science and conducting his own gold-standard studies on everything from fermented foods to fish oil.
But when, after two years of work, the committee submitted its 400-page report, it was summarily dismissed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the Trump administration’s new health secretary, and his team.
points: Christopher Gardner, the author of Food Sense and director of nutrition studies at Stanford, says we have overcomplicated the question of what to eat.

articles.title: I hate golf | Adrian Chiles
articles.summary: I’ve been trying to quit the game for years. Just when I thought I was out, it pulled me back in … I hate golf. A good walk spoiled? The whole day spoiled, more like. As with many cases of hate, it has its roots in love. You see, I just love the feeling of hitting the ball sweetly.
body: My logic ran that if I could play like that as an absolute beginner, imagine what I could do with a bit of practice. I strode up to my ball on the fairway and, swinging with great confidence, played an air shot. Missed it completely. Pretending this was but my practice swing, I tried again, and this time made contact with the ball, but mostly with the ground, causing lasting damage to the fairway. The ball advanced all of six inches. Welcome to golf.

That a complete novice can hit a proper shot is both the best thing about golf and the worst. It draws you in, giving you great encouragement. But it also drives you nuts when, unaccountably, you suddenly can’t do it. Other skills aren’t like this. Take the piano. To play even just the slow opening bit of Beethoven’s Pathétique Sonata would take years of practice. Nobody ever sat at a piano, with no experience, and on day one played anything resembling Beethoven. Yet in golf, it is kind of possible. And it’s equally possible, moments later, to find yourself quite incapable of doing anything of the sort.

articles.title: I went to a Jamaican Patois class. Why was I so scared to speak it?
articles.summary: Centuries of historical baggage surrounds this form of speech. But I’m vowing to overcome shame and connect with this part of my culture. Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here.
body: Recently, my sister sent me and my mum a graphic promoting a Jamaican Patois (or Patwa) class on Instagram, organised by British teacher and author Naia Lewis. It was unlike anything I’d ever seen before – Patois and other Caribbean Creole forms of speech are rarely treated as legitimate languages.

As a descendant of Caribbean migrants to the UK, I grew up surrounded by Patois, but had never practised speaking it. I wanted to go, but felt terrified of embarrassing myself. This week, I conquered that fear and explored why learning Patois and other Creole languages is so fraught and controversial across the diaspora.

articles.title: I spent months taste-testing 15 tinned fish varieties. These are the ones I’d eat again
articles.summary: Is it possible to get tired of eating tinned fish? From Fishwife tuna to Wildfish salmon, I ate tinned fish 15 different ways. The 10 best (and worst) whey protein powders – taste-tested. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: A s a child, I often wrinkled my nose at the humble cans of anchovies and salmon that my grandparents diligently stocked in their pantry, wondering why they would choose a cold chunk instead of a freshly baked fillet. But in recent years, tinned fish has undergone a facelift. The pungent anchovies people have avoided like the plague are now a coveted consumable.

While tinned fish has been around for ages, its popularity is a relatively recent phenomenon. Brands such as Fishwife, launched in 2020, have turned conservas into a status symbol, collaborating with chains such as Sweetgreen and celebrities such as gen Z musician Audrey Hobert. More unique offerings such as oysters and mackerel have entered the mainstream too.

“There are all these cool brands now that are so easy to find in grocery stores. I think that has urged people to be more curious and give it a try,” says Anna Hezel, the author of Tin to Table, a cookbook featuring more than 50 ways to eat tinned fish.

This crawl took place on a Saturday in September, filled with drinks and snacks (but mostly bites of bar burgers), working our way from Santa Monica to Manhattan Beach before wandering inland for dinner in Torrance, home to some of the best Japanese food in the United States.

The plan was to start relatively early, enjoying as much sunlit ocean breeze as we could, while also allowing me to get a normal amount of sleep at the end of the night before waking up at traditional dad hours. articles.title: Céline Dion’s Chanel Look Nods to Her 1997 Oscars Dress—and Took 1,380 Hours to Make
articles.summary: The star wore a custom Chanel gown that nodded back to her glitzy red-carpet look at the 1997 Oscars.
body: Last month, Celine Dion made her glorious return to the stage in Paris, following a years-long private battle with stiff-person syndrome (SPS). And what a return it was: The iconic French Canadian singer has been hitting the stage at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, France, exiting her hotel before each performance wearing a different high-fashion look, and then hitting the stage in similarly buzzy outfits, including custom Dior and Givenchy, among others.

This evening, however, Dion closed out her final week of shows (until May 2027, when she picks the tour back up) on an even more fabulous fashion note: The star opened her concert tonight wearing a custom Chanel dress that was inspired by the glitzy gown she wore back at the 1997 Oscars.

Back at the ’97 awards show, Dion made history when she became the first artist to perform twice during the same Oscars ceremony. (She sang her own hit “Because You Loved Me,” and a cover of Barbara Streisand’s “I Finally Found Someone.”) The star did so in a glitzy, silver plunging Chanel gown and comet-style necklace from Chanel, designed by Karl Lagerfeld, the brand’s designer at the time.

articles.title: Chicago’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Is Cooking From 900-Year-Old Recipes
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants.
body: Zubair Mohajir is one of Chicago’s most prolific new chefs and restaurateurs, behind such openings as Lilac Tiger, Mariela, Mirra, Sarima, and most recently, Muhājir, a restaurant that traces historical spice routes to tell the story of global migration. I talked to Mohajir about how the opening is going, how he thinks about collaboration across his different projects, and why Muhājir is finally the restaurant that feels like home.

Zubair Mohajir: Muhājir is such a personal story for me, because my last name is Mohajir, and the meaning of “muhājir” in Arabic and Urdu is “one who migrates.” When the partition [of India and Pakistan] happened, the Muslims that were moved from India to Pakistan were named Muhājirs because they were migrated. In my family, we always wondered why that was our last name. When I started cooking [after working in finance], it really started to settle in. Our late maternal grandfather was obsessed with mapping where this family name came from. It comes from Southern Basra, Iraq, and that was so mind-blowing for me because it’s one of the biggest spice roads.

articles.title: On Her Upcoming Third Album, Charlotte Cardin Is Ready to Take On the World
articles.summary: The Canadian musician has already conquered France and Canada—but with the ravishing ‘Midnight, Mon Amour,’ the rest of the world should be taking notice.
body: When Charlotte Cardin appears on screen from Paris, she’s almost at the end of the fashion week whirlwind. Once upon a time, the Canadian singer-songwriter could be found on the runways herself: back in the mid-2010s, she even walked for the likes of Jacquemus and Christopher Kane. Thanks to her Jane Birkin cheekbones and statuesque height, she continues to find herself pulled into the industry’s orbit, even well over a decade into her career as a musician—this season, she took in the Saint Laurent show from the front row. Right now, however, she’s ready to focus on the music. “Mostly promo and the album announcement,” she says, smiling. “All of that fun stuff.”

After all, Cardin—who divides her life between Paris and her hometown of Montreal—is on the precipice of a new chapter. On Friday, she unveiled her slinky, retro-tinged new single, “Memories” (alongside a twin-track French counterpart, “Souvenir,” but more on that later). And more crucially, it serves as the official introduction to her ambitious third studio album, Midnight, Mon Amour, announced this week and set for release on January 29 via The Orchard and Cult Nation.
points: The Canadian musician has already conquered France and Canada—but with the ravishing ‘Midnight, Mon Amour,’ the rest of the world should be taking notice.

articles.title: How “Skillcations” Became One of the Year’s Biggest Travel Trends
articles.summary: Here’s why there’s a boom in travelers taking vacations specifically to learn a new skill or hobby—and some of the best places to do it.
body: My body goes limp as water gushes around me. When I finally emerge, taking in a sharp breath while smiling at my instructor through salt-stung eyes, I can’t help but think, “This is way better than a spa day.” I’ve just caught my first wave in Bali after a multi-day surf workshop at Uluwatu Surf Villas. Even though it was just a five-second ride, the thrill of being bad at something, then getting slightly better, has me chasing the next one.

And it’s not just surfing. Over the years, I’ve increasingly dedicated trips to learning something new. I’ve clumsily thrown myself into swing dancing lessons in Italy, freediving sessions in French Polynesia, and Spanish intensives in Ecuador. I came home from each one feeling a little more capable than when I arrived.

Apparently, I’m not alone. “Skillcations,” as the travel industry has dubbed them, are gaining traction. Mastercard Inc. research published in July found that nearly half of people surveyed were planning a trip to learn a skill. Meanwhile, a 2026 trends report by Hilton Worldwide Holdings Inc. found that 72% of travelers wanted to take time off to pursue a personal passion or hobby.

articles.title: The Kazakh Designers Telling Stories of Their Nomadic Heritage
articles.summary: Looking to reconnect with her Almaty origins, writer Yulia Denisyuk heads to the Kazakh capital to meet artists exploring their own identities through craft.
body: The summers I spent in Almaty form some of my sweetest childhood memories. I was born in Kazakhstan’s former capital (and still its largest city) and moved to Estonia in 1986, at age three, returning every school break into my teenage years. Once I relocated to the United States in the early 2000s, the frequent visits stopped. In my preliminary years overseas, I handled bouts of nostalgia by conjuring up those memories: eating ice cream below the mosaicked swallows of Qarlygash Cafe (which means swallow in Kazakh) near my grandmother’s apartment, or catching rare glimpses of felt-covered yurts in the foothills of the Tian Shan mountains from my grandfather’s Zhiguli sedan.

Decades in the US have since turned my Kazakh past into something distant, but as I’ve grown older—and watched my loved ones in Almaty age, too—I’ve yearned to regain a link to my origins. So this year, I returned, hoping to reconnect with the landscapes and motifs of Kazakhstan that I still hold dear, and to meet the crop of young Kazakh artists who, like me, are increasingly examining their own identities through them.

articles.title: I Want My Sons to Know What Happened to Me
articles.summary: “I want my sons to know what I experienced,” writes Anna Sullivan. “They need to understand that rape doesn’t happen only in dark parking garages—it happens everywhere, and sometimes between people who know each other. It happens to people you know, people you love. It happened to me.”
body: Recently, while driving my son and a few of his friends to soccer practice, one of them used the word “chopped” to describe a girl from their class.
“Don’t say that,” I said, knowing full well it was Gen Alpha slang for unattractive.
Later, on the drive home, careful to avoid direct eye contact in the rearview mirror, I brought it up again.
“You cannot talk about people that way, especially girls,” I said. I wasn’t sure of the point I was trying to make, but I noticed the swell rising in my chest, flooding my nervous system.
